summary: Specifies how to use the SHA-256 digest type in DNSSEC Delegation Signer (DS) records. DS records in a parent zone point to DNSKEYs in a child zone. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A stronger fingerprint method for the card in the parent that vouches for the child, so forgers have a harder time.

questions: what is a ds record digest type
what is digest type 2 in dnssec
subtitle: How DNSSEC parent zones can publish a SHA-256 fingerprint of a child zone's key instead of only a SHA-1 one.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC Delegation Signer (DS) records hold a digest of a child zone's key, and a stronger digest than SHA-1 was wanted.
tldr.mechanism: Digest type code 2 is assigned to SHA-256, computed over the DNSKEY owner name and RDATA and published untruncated as a 32 byte value in the DS record.
tldr.outcome: Implementations MUST support SHA-256 in DS records, and zone operators are encouraged to deploy it, possibly alongside SHA-1 records for a while.

today: RFC 4509 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines digest type 2 for DS records.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In DNSSEC (RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035), a parent zone publishes a DS resource record to distribute a cryptographic digest of one key in a child zone's DNSKEY RRset.

The DS RRset is signed by at least one of the parent zone's private zone data signing keys for each algorithm the parent uses. Each signature is published in an RRSIG record with the same owner name as the DS RRset and a type covered of DS. This document adds SHA-256 as a digest option for DS records.
sections.eli5: A parent zone writes down a short fingerprint of its child's key. This RFC lets it use a newer way to make that fingerprint.

sections.title: SHA-256 as a DS Digest Type
sections.content:
Digest type code 2 is assigned to SHA-256 for use in DS records. The result of the digest MUST NOT be truncated, and the entire 32 byte result is published in the DS record.

The digest is computed as SHA_256(DNSKEY owner name | DNSKEY RDATA), where | means concatenation and the DNSKEY RDATA is defined by RFC 4034 as Flags, Protocol, Algorithm and Public Key joined together. The Key Tag and Algorithm fields are unchanged and stay as specified in RFC 4034.
sections.eli5: You mix the key's name and the key itself into a blender and get a fixed-size fingerprint. You keep the whole fingerprint and do not cut any off.

sections.title: Wire Format and Example
sections.content:
On the wire, a DS record using SHA-256 carries the Key Tag, the Algorithm, a Digest Type field set to 2, and then the digest, which is 32 bytes long for SHA-256.

The RFC gives an example based on the DNSKEY/DS records in section 5.4 of RFC 4034. The key dskey.example.com. has key id 60485, and its matching DS record reads 60485 5 2 followed by the hexadecimal digest.
sections.eli5: The DS record is a small label with the key's number, the kind of lock it belongs to, which fingerprint recipe was used, and then the fingerprint itself.

sections.title: Implementation Requirements
sections.content: Implementations MUST support the use of SHA-256 in DS records. Validator implementations SHOULD ignore DS records containing SHA-1 digests if DS records with SHA-256 digests are present in the same DS RRset.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to learn the new fingerprint recipe. If both an old and a new fingerprint are present, checkers should prefer the new one.

sections.title: Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
If a validator does not support SHA-256 and no other DS record in the RRset has a supported digest type, the validator has no supported authentication path from parent to child. The resolver should then treat this like an authenticated NSEC RRset proving that no DS RRset exists, as described in section 5.2 of RFC 4035.

Zone administrators cannot control how fast validators gain SHA-256 support, so operators should consider deploying both SHA-1 and SHA-256 DS records for every DNSKEY that gets DS records. Whether to use both digest types, and for how long, is a policy decision outside the scope of the document.
sections.eli5: Some checkers are slow to learn the new recipe, so a school might keep both the old and new fingerprint on file until everyone catches up.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The only IANA action is that the digest type for SHA-256 in DS records has been assigned. At the time of writing, the assigned digest types are listed in the table below.
sections.eli5: There is an official list of fingerprint recipes, and the new one now has its own number on it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A downgrade attack from a stronger digest type to a weaker one is possible if a zone has several DS records for one child DNSKEY with different digest types, and a validator accepts a weaker digest even when a stronger one is present but invalid. For example, if the SHA-1 digest matches the child's DNSKEY but the SHA-256 digest does not, a validator that treats this as secure effectively ignores the stronger digest.

Users of DNSSEC are encouraged to deploy SHA-256 as soon as software allows. SHA-256 is widely believed to be more resilient to attack than SHA-1, and confidence in SHA-1 was being eroded by recently announced attacks. The RFC considers SHA-256 sufficiently strong for the immediate future, but says future attacks may weaken it, and it does not speculate further.
sections.eli5: If a thief can pick the weak lock when a strong lock is also on the door, the strong lock is pointless. Checkers must not let the weak fingerprint win when the strong one disagrees.
